paragraphs: Ivan Karp Edited

Okay. So, first, can you just tell me about the first time that you met Maurice Sievan? I don't remember the exact occasion. I was employed at a fine arts gallery in Provincetown, Massachusetts. And those who were in residence in the community used to come in regularly to see the exhibitions also, to submit evidence of their work in hopes of an exhibition. And I think from the very beginning of my acquaintance with him, I was very responsive to what he'd been doing. Really nothing to do with his character personality, which was also in many ways attractive to me. But his work already was singular and remarkable and mature, totally mature work. Occupied it, in my mind, a very special place. It didn't relate distinctly to any other prevailing trends. In that sense, he was an innovator of a surprisingly private vision. So as a person, when you first met him, did he strike you as being different? I don't really know that much. I never met him myself.

Having dealt with artists most of my mature life, there's a broad range of personality, character involved in this, And I don't think he was outside of the general range or personality type as far as it goes. He was a fairly insular person. I wouldn't call him buoyant or spirited. But he was a man in complete control of his vision. He had something clear in his mind in his theory of art and what had to be done. And he seemed to be always unwavering from that. He was totally dedicated to his craft.
I need to stop just a second. (unintelligible).
Now, you talked about some of the qualities of his work when you first saw his work and things stood out. Can you give me an idea?

Well, the paintings had a kind of a mystical, almost a haunted character, as if there was some kind of vision pressing through even the conscious workings of the artist himself. Of course, this is often the case with certain kinds of imagery, but it was more intensely so with him, and as it was couched in a kind of very fine, elegant style, it struck me as something worthy of being seriously considered by the audience.
Can you describe Maurice Sievan, the artist?

I have just now just a dim recollection. I had not seen him for over 12, 14 years. And I just remember his physical being and his temperament. And that's, as I say, a vague outline as far as that goes. It's just I can say that it was a man whose whole life was his work. And totally dedicated. He was constantly pursuing the next theory, the next idea, the next principle, the next painting. That was the function of his life, you know. He was also a man of a affable social demeanor, right? And we had a very nice personal relationship. Okay, great. Can you share any anecdotes about Maurice? I know you were out in Provincetown together.

I don't remember a singular occurrence that one would be considered memorable. I just know that I enjoyed being with him and being fascinated by his dedication to his life's career. We spent some social hours together, and they were always very amiable. And he was, of course, very much delighted with the fact that there was a—at that time I was a younger person, a young, zealous, passionate member of the art community interested in his work. Did you ever spend time at his studio? Did you see him painting ever? You know, in the curiously long career that I've had in the visual arts, about 35 years, I've never been in the studio of the artist while he was actually at work, and I always preferred that in a way. I always liked the idea that the process of making the work was a kind of mysterious thing and that I would not see the object until it was completed. And it's been like that all through my career. I expect I had visited his studio on several occasions, It's all work possibly in progress and completed, but I never saw him actually in the working process. I know when he was on Provincetown, he was renting out Rothko's studio at the time, and I was wondering if you had ever spent time with him and Rothko or maybe or other people. Oh, I knew all the artists then. The art world was, of course, very much dominated in the early 60s, late 50s, by the abstract expressionist movement. And, of course, we all had the same heroes, you know. And, of course, Rothko was one of the persons who dominated the spectrum of powerful American art, of Klein, de Kooning, Rothko, Franz Klein, was in Provincetown also for a very brief interval, and I knew him. I knew all of these people to a degree. Rothko was a very detached, very, very insular person. It wasn't easy to become amiable with him, you know.
Maurice, in that sense, was just quite the opposite. He was a very affectionate, very warm person.

Are there times that you can remember out there where Maurice was with these people? Only, I can only remember being together with them, but perhaps at a social occasion in the arts where there may have been a local opening of an arts event, you know. There were several of those. In this community in Provincetown, there were a lot of luminaries there in the art world. We're still a very insular community, and there's a lot of little local politics and a lot of petty things occurring all the time, you know. And there were these social events, and everybody would turn up for them and behave reasonably well. I'm hearing as I'm learning more about Maurice that he did spend a lot of time with Rothko and Milton Avery. They not only shared studio space, but they vacationed together and things like that. Trying to get a sense of that, kind of a first-hand sense of people who might have been there.

He never told me much about his relationship with those people. He may have. In fact, I may have overlooked that. you know so I say I knew both Rothko and Avery and they were both very subdued characters as far as it goes I imagine in the sense of Rothko's personality that there was a lot of hidden turmoil very very intense person really and the other Avery was not like that he was a very gentle very mild man who had a very nice social poise you know always looked very charming very elegant you know I didn't know Maurice's involvement with them he may have made reference to that
you know... ...chairs are so old.
Yeah, it's a lot of noise from us people.

But once I have, I have to do a camera and ask questions today. Now, can you tell me, give me a little bit of a historical perspective on the New York school artists in the 40s, 50s, and 60s, and also possibly tell me, how does Maurice fit in with that?

The fact of the matter is that Maurice didn't fit in at all, and he could never be considered as part of the general entourage of painters who had achieved notoriety and fame, and whose notoriety, as I say, probably occurred not until the late 50s, but until the middle of the late 50s.

There had been no clearly identified American school in the post-war period except for the abstract expressionists, you know. As I say, they were very much dominated by the great forceful work of people like de Kooning, Klein, Rothko, and Motherwell to a degree who was living in Provincetown until his very late life, as far as I know. Maurice was an outsider in that sense, and he would always function that way through all of his career. His work did not connect up distinctly to any prevailing trend. and that made it much more difficult for him to advance his career because the audience, and especially in the 50s, was extremely small. The audience for contemporary art is still small, you know. But at that time, you could number it to 25 to 50 people who really were responsive distinctly to contemporary art and might acquire something. He was an outsider, so he didn't really connect up. There were aspects of his work that related to expressionism, yet there were images in his work, and the abstract expressionists really stayed clear of imagery, you know. It seemed at that time the only heroic kind of work you could do had to be abstract art. And if you did figurative work, you were considered either reactionary or gross eccentric. In that sense, Maurice's work was really outside the pale of common acceptance. It was like that most of his career. So you wouldn't consider him as one of the vanguard artists? He wasn't an acclaimed vanguard artist, but you could say he was vanguard in the sense that he was an inventor and that he opened territory that he himself explored, you know. In that sense, he was an innovator, you know.

Okay. Can you tell me about some of the exhibits that you were involved with? I had only shown his work in Provincetown at the gallery with which I was connected, and I wrote a very brief introduction to an exhibition that he had here somewhere in Manhattan. I think that was in the 60s. I don't recall the date of that, but I was very proud to do that for him. I didn't see him very often in the city. He'd come by and say hello every so often. I may have gone to his studio once or twice. I don't remember clearly that I did. But I was always a work and alert to the shows that he was having and always attended them. And I always felt that his work was singular and worthy of public playing.

I was going through their files the other day and I saw a note that a letter that Lee Sievan had was sending to the Whitney, I think. And there were a number of signatures, and yours was one of the signatures, urging them to consider him for a show.
Well, of course, we do that on behalf of our own artists and other artists as well. And

unfortunately, the people who manage and run museums, the curators at the records of museums, are not always awake or alert to the very best of what's happening. Either the information doesn't get to them, or they don't have the capacity to adjudge the merits of things, which is unfortunate. that it's a permeating characteristic of museum officials, that they're not always equipped to adjudge the best work being produced in their time. And they're also distinctly subject to prevailing trends, you know, and popular personalities. In that sense, Maurice couldn't enter the sphere because he wasn't outreaching in that way. He wasn't a man who went to all the social occasions in the arts and who made demands on leading characters in the art world. He just basically did his work, you know, and he was heroic in that regard, you know. But people like Maurice, and there are many others like that, don't make the kind of dramatic progress in their careers or as rapidly as some who are more vivid personality types and who reach out in their careers, you know.

Right. If you could advise a director of a museum, I won't even say, you know, any specific museum, but just obviously he, you know, he had a show at the MIC Museum in North Carolina, And he had a show at the Queens Museum in 1974, which was somewhat after the facts towards him through this life. If you could, if a museum official were to ask you, what would you think?

I could speak with strong conviction about his place in American art and certainly of his worthiness to be included in an exhibition of the artists of his time. And he certainly is worthy of a one-person event of some consequence. He's an artist who contributed in a singular way to the American fine arts culture.

That's great. Why is it that Maurice Sievan's work never made an impact? Well, all the factors that I've described to you feed into the fact that he'd been left in the shadows. The first, his character type is a man very subdued, very laid back, very insular. His work being outside the mainstream, right? The inability of himself or his wife, who was very dedicated to him, to enter into the political turmoil of American art world activity. You know, that's something that you really have to do if you want to make rapid progress. More than anything else, that his work did not distinctly connect up to prevailing trends. It was always singular, always, as you might even say on the outside, eccentric. You know, private vision. And private visionaries only very rarely can make the kind of career progress that other artists make.
Yeah, it seems to me, just as an outsider, that some of the people who are considered to be the

greatest artists had their own, followed their own paths and did their own path. I don't know who you're referring to. Most of those artists who've achieved major attention in the United States in the last 30 or 40 years, which is the period that I'm acquainted with, were connected up to some prevailing trend in the arts, you know. Whereas if they were outside the mainstream, then they themselves were very vivid characters. Their personalities were able to make an imprint on the politics of the art community.
Like Jackson Pollock.

Well, Jackson Pollock of Warhol was certainly one of the characters that you must describe as part of the pop art movement. He and Liechtenstein and Westelman and Oldenburg are leaders of that movement, and they've been associated together as a philosophical group, as it were, you know. So the same with Jackson Pollock as the harbinger of abstract expressionism, right? And he connects up to de Kooning, Klein, Rothko, and so forth as part of an American fine arts movement. But Maurice could never be that, right? His work just did not connect up that way. There were intimations, as I say, of his responsiveness to certain things in prevailing moods in the arts. but he remained a singular practitioner.
Could it be that Maurice might have been the leader of a figurative movement of his own that never got discovered?

He could have become that if he'd gotten proper exposure and young formative artists had been properly acquainted with the work. His work could have inspired younger artists. But I don't think on a broad spectrum because, as I say, the work came out of his very singular character. He was not responsive to the world so much outside of himself. He was not an observer of the landscape in the traditional sense, right? They were all basically mystical, inward, and singular, you know. And that's hard to find a movement developing around that kind of thing.

If there was a movement that he would have been the leader of, how would you describe? I couldn't come up with an appellation, proper describing term for what his work was, right? It was a private vision, the only way you can describe it.
Okay. Do you consider Maurice Sievan as an average painter, a great painter, and a great
painter, and one?

His technical mastery of his craft had achieved total maturity. So in that sense, he's an artist of accomplishment just for that alone. the fact that he could merge a private vision with his extended craftability makes him an artist of singular achievement an artist of some consequence
I'm going to just turn probably already covered this but I'll ask it anyway why do some very good artists make it while other very good artists don't?

This is one of the distresses that people of idealistic outlook have to confront. It's the truth in every arts profession, dance, in the theater, in literature, in the music, you know, that those who enter into this creative enterprise, whose character, his physical character, who is perhaps their physical charm, their ability to reach out into the community they're functioning in, is of a high degree of intensity, make more progress in their careers more rapidly. Achieving notoriety on merit alone has to be a slow process for those who are totally dedicated to their craft and don't enter continuously into the social arena of their chosen profession. Okay. Do you think that, I mean, now we're starting to show Maurice's work, and hopefully there'll be an ongoing slew of shows and exhibits. Do you think that when Sievan's work is exhibited now, that he will be recognized in the history books of modern era? I think if this material, this production is properly portrayed, that is exhibited, that there could be an awakening to the fact that he was there and that he is worthy of the interest that the fine arts community should give to an artist like himself. It could come to pass. Were you involved at all in any museum acquisitions? of Maurice's work? Well, I don't know what you mean by museum acquisitions. I don't play any part in doing anything here at this gallery except offering works through exhibitions and with great expectations that perhaps museum persons will turn up here and acquire things, but I was never able to, in any significant way, bring his work to significant public attention. So I know that there are about seven or eight museums that have his work in permanent...
No, I didn't play any technical role in placing those works. Okay. Do you happen to know about the Museum of Modern Art that he's a studying Museum of Modern Art?
I'm just acquainted with the fact that it's there. I don't know the mechanism wherein it achieved that position.

Okay. Now, when you exhibited Maurice's paintings, what did you tell prospective buyers? obviously there's always some kind of self-picture you have to tell your clients about an artist. Well, as I say, there's the cognizantity of the art world. Those who know what they're looking at, they don't really need much guidance whatsoever. For those who might be confounded by confrontation with a particular kind of object, then there's certainly a kind of statement that goes with it in trying to describe what the artist's attributes are and trying to explain why this particular artist has been selected for exhibition. And you always talk about the emergence, at least I do. I always talk about the ability of the artist to merge his technical abilities with a singular vision. And that's what I would describe in the case of Maurice, right? That it was obviously on the level of virtuoso technical skill. And the work occupied a very special place in vision. This is the best you can say for somebody.
Yeah.
And I think I need to change tapes.
Okay. Okay. Do you have any pictures of Maurice at home or around the studio that you can remember or paintings of this?

No, I may have a sketch in my vast archives. Of course, I've been, as I say, 35 years doing this, and I've received things from artists over the years, sketches and drawings and little mementos, and there's a vast archive, but I've not perused it in a long time. I don't know if anything Maurice is in that.
Yeah, one of the reasons why I asked was because we're in the process of photographing everything.

Oh, everything there is. Yeah, I'll do the proper request for you. Yeah, anything that might be worthy of yours. We might be putting a book together in the future. That would be great. Now, just for a historical perspective, maybe you can help me out on this. Can you tell me what the WPA program did for American artists? Well, during that terribly stressful economic interval, there was fortunately an awareness on the part of certain government agencies that the artists also were participants in American life. And there was a program generated to employ artists as best could be in connection with government projects. And it was a remarkable thing to have occurred during a very, very painful, very stressful period in American life. So I can say that to a degree, it was a successful program just by its instigation alone. And the fact that a number of artists did get managed finally to participate on some level in producing objects, it was an encouragement to the nature of their life to participate as artists in the American economy. It was a significant thing for the government and for the artists. It was a wonderful thing to have happened. I don't remember it that clearly. I was still in my formative years when these projects were underway. okay now in the book that I told you I was reading about the art biz I read in one of the chapters that you told Andy Warhol came in with a pack of a Brillo and he gave him a can of Campbell's soup and said here paint this

that's not entirely accurate the fact of the matter is that Andy was always solicitous of ideas about his work one of those very modest people in a way who used to ask me, what should I do now? And there was always wonderful things around his studio, but he was never satisfied that he had touched on the significant kernel of a new vision. And he would ask all of his friends and me regularly about what objects or what things or what visions were worthy of his particular abilities. That happened a number of times. There were several images that I supplied him with, but that wasn't one of them. The soup came, were already in his studio when I visited for the first time, so that's not technically accurate about our relationship. Okay, but actually what I was wondering from that is was there ever a time that Maurice asked you about ideas?

Oh no, not Maurice. Maurice never needed anybody to inspire him to what kind of images he should deal with. They were crowding into his mind at all times. He had more than he could possibly deal with. Right.

Okay. if you can remember what is your favorite Sievan painting well there's one painting that's always stayed with me it's a depiction of a human presence would seem to be a male presence without clear delineation of facial characteristics or body parts just essentially an outline in big black gestures that connects up in some way to the momentum of abstract expression and expressionist picture. And it had some real scale that was probably the size of human presence. And it was a work of tremendous eloquence. And that's always stayed with me, that particular painting.
Do you remember the name of it?

He invented the terms for his paintings. He invented words. And I used to ask him about that all the time. He said, it's just something that seemed to be consonant with the object or with the image or with the figure that he was dealing with, you know. I don't remember that, no. I see, I think I can see it here, even from the back. This is one very much close, very, very much like it. And this one over here that's very much like it also on the right side here. The other's not, but these two are very close to that particular image. And this one is called Grunix, and the other one is called Epsiphon. That's what I'm saying about his odd usage of titles here. Those two are very close to the one that I'm speaking of, which was a single image. Well, these are double images. but they're both pictures of tremendous strength and character. Now, while you have those over there, I was wondering if you would mind just on each of them or any of them that you would like, just kind of telling us something about them or why they're strong-handed.

Well, what's evident in all of his work is his consonants, is that there's an ongoing unity of vision in the work, is that you can identify the signatory... artist here that you know it's a sea man it's not likely to be anybody else and though he probably like as all artists are influenced by outside elements here uh this is a very private vision and it has continuity and that's what's remarkable about it you know is that it can't be anybody else it's Maurice you know are there any specific pieces in there that you could uh uh I don't know there's I idon't think that there have been much uh analysis done on any of these kind of paintings or, you know. Well, all paintings have psychological content, and if you wanted to speculate on the meaning

of things, you could take this pretty far because there's a lot of so-called haunted elements in here. There's some reference to, in some of these nature pictures here where there are flowers and mystical sunrises. It's a little bit like Odilon Redon in there. There was a mystical strain all through Maurice's work, and they have a ghostly presence at times, And which is the ghost of the artist himself, his own unconscious, peering through in the canvas, you know. I see that in all of his work.

That one on the bottom is actually the last self-portrait that he did as oil on canvas. He did others after that that were very small and started getting much more gruesome as time went on. but I'm trying to interest the time.
(unintelligible)
Okay. Did Maurice ever talk with you about Kierkegaard or metaphysics or anything along those lines?

I suspect that it's probably something that was part of our conversation, was his convictions and his beliefs, his philosophy, his outlook, his theories, his intellectual pursuits. Those things probably cropped up regularly. But I don't remember any particular conversation in which we discussed issues like that.
Now, Maurice Seabound died 10 years ago. If you were to write an epitaph, what would you say?

Lovely question. I would say that there is an artist who occupied a particular and very special place in the history of American painting and who is worthy of public acclaim for his singular achievement.
Is it possible for you to say that again without your hand?

I would say that the artist was worthy of national recognition for his remarkable maturity of craftsmanship and the ongoing singular quality of his vision. That's great. Just one more question, and I think that this probably will even cover it more than cover it. Clement Greenberg said that Maurice Sievan was the best American artist in the 20's,

Well, you know, the fact of the matter is that I wasn't acquainted with his work until the 1960s or late 50s, you know. And late 50s it was, early 60s. And the only work that I saw was work produced during that interval. I didn't know of his achievement of the 30s and 40s at all. He never showed me anything from that period. And it's possible that I might have agreed with Mr. Greenberg about that achievement. A lot of good painters during that period. So that's a very, very strong statement.
That was a very strong statement.
Yeah.
So, okay. That's great.
My pleasure, indeed.
